cells.tense: You are standing where new things arrive, and the shape of what's coming is already clear to you.
cells.ask: Say the conclusion you already hold out loud, then show the two steps that got you there — before the day ends, once, to one person.
cells.core: Something comes in — a problem, an offer, a shift in someone's mood — and it doesn't stay blurry for you. You cut to what it is fast, and the cut usually holds. That move is running well right now. You don't have to prove it anymore, so let it show. Sharpening it further isn't the work. Letting it be seen is. Say the conclusion you already hold out loud, then show the two steps that got you there, once, before the day ends. It isn't a performance. The work is done. Let the fact of it reach the person across from you.
cells.sheetLine: You see what's arriving before most do. Let it land too.
cells.verb: cutting through noise to the shape of the thing
cells.place: the threshold where what's coming in first gets met

cells.tense: You are three conclusions ahead of what has actually arrived, bracing for a conversation no one has started.
cells.ask: Pick one worry you've already solved in your head and put the planning down for this afternoon — no notes, no rehearsal, just the afternoon.
cells.core: The clean version is one conclusion and then a stop — you read what arrived and leave space for the next thing. You let the other person bring their half instead of delivering both parts. Right now something small comes in and it's already a whole scenario: what they'll say, what you'll answer, where it goes. The thinking is good. There's just too much of it, spending you on arrivals that haven't happened. Set down one afternoon of planning nobody asked for. Not to be less sharp — so what you're sharp at meets what's here instead of what you've already built.
cells.sheetLine: You've solved a conversation nobody has started yet.

cells.tense: The shape of the thing was legible, it was called out once, and since then the door has been quiet.
cells.ask: Tell one person the thing that took you years to understand, in plain words, this week — even if it comes out rough.
cells.core: The door is still there, and nothing is being read at it. Something shows up and it stays fuzzy, or gets answered with whatever's loudest rather than what you actually see. You've been quiet at the door since your reading got said out loud and landed wrong. Passing on what you know is what revives the reading — teaching, putting an idea where someone else can use it. You have hard-won understanding sitting unused. Hand one piece of it to one person this week, rough, unpolished, alive. It isn't to sharpen them. It's to put you back at the door where you read.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped calling the shape. Hand one piece back.

cells.tense: You are already reading what arrives and calling it nothing in particular.
cells.ask: Ask one person to name a call you made this week that turned out right, and take it in without waving it off.
cells.core: You read what's coming in — you catch the direction early, you sort what matters from what doesn't, you cut to the point for the room. Then you talk like it was obvious, or just the news, or anyone would have said the same. People lean on your read and rarely hear you claim it. Being met is what brings it back. Ask one person to tell you a call you made this week that turned out right, and hear it in their words without waving it off. Not a compliment hunt — someone reflecting your own work back so you can pick it up.
cells.sheetLine: You're already reading the room. You keep calling it the news.

attempts.check: The one unsupported claim is that strategic thinking is 'entering now' — the record has the seat, but not the person's timing or what arrived. The reader could reasonably say this is their ordinary mind, not a turning point. The asks do not depend on the read happening: saying a conclusion and reasoning it, holding one afternoon to plan, passing on a hard-won idea, or repeating someone's words and explaining, all stand if the read is wrong. The sentence that serves the writer is 'You're the one who sees the shape of it first' — it flatters without evidence, and has been cut.
